metadata.title: Inverse Trigonometry, Elevation, Depression, and Bearings
metadata.vcaa_description: Use trigonometric ratios and Pythagoras' theorem to solve right-angled triangle problems.
metadata.target_mastery: Use inverse trigonometric functions ($\sin^{-1}, \cos^{-1}, \tan^{-1}$) to find acute angles and solve applied problems involving angles of elevation, depression, and three-figure true bearings.
prerequisites: Alternate angles on parallel lines (Year 8 VC2M8M05)

key_vocabulary.definition: The inverse operations (also written $\arcsin, \arccos, \arctan$) that recover an unknown acute angle $\theta$ from a known side ratio: e.g., if $\sin\theta = \frac{O}{H}$, then $\theta = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{O}{H}\right)$.
The upward angle through which an observer's line of sight is raised from the horizontal line when looking up at an elevated object.
The downward angle through which an observer's line of sight is lowered from the horizontal line when looking down at an object below.

A direction angle measured clockwise from True North ($000^\circ\text{T}$), always written using three digits from $000^\circ\text{T}$ to $360^\circ\text{T}$ (e.g., due East is $090^\circ\text{T}$ and South-West is $225^\circ\text{T}$).

theory.title: Finding Unknown Acute Angles Using Inverse Trigonometry
theory.explanation: When two side lengths of a right-angled triangle are known, we find an unknown acute angle $\theta$ by first writing the appropriate trigonometric ratio ($\sin\theta = \frac{O}{H}$, $\cos\theta = \frac{A}{H}$, or $\tan\theta = \frac{O}{A}$) and then applying the corresponding inverse trigonometric function ($\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$, or $\tan^{-1}$). Note that the superscript $-1$ in $\sin^{-1}$ denotes the inverse function, NOT the reciprocal $\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$.
theory.callout_title: Check that Your Calculator Is in DEGREES Mode
theory.callout_rule: Before evaluating any trigonometric or inverse trigonometric expression in Year 9, check that your calculator screen displays 'DEG' (or 'D'). For example, $\sin^{-1}(0.5)$ must return $30^\circ$.

theory.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
theory.explanation: Both the angle of elevation (looking UP) and the angle of depression (looking DOWN) are ALWAYS measured from a horizontal reference line, never from a vertical wall or cliff. Because the horizontal line at the top observer and the horizontal ground at the bottom object are parallel, the angle of depression from $A$ down to $B$ equals the angle of elevation from $B$ up to $A$ (alternate angles in a 'Z' configuration on parallel lines).
theory.formula_latex: \text{Angle of depression from } A \text{ to } B = \text{Angle of elevation from } B \text{ to } A \; (\text{alternate angles})
theory.callout_title: Always Draw the Horizontal Dotted Line First
theory.callout_rule: The angle of depression is between the top HORIZONTAL line and the line of sight. If a question gives an angle of depression $\theta$, draw a horizontal dotted line at the top or transfer $\theta$ into the bottom corner as the equal alternate angle of elevation.

theory.title: Compass and True Bearings in Navigation
theory.explanation: A three-figure true bearing ($\text{NNN}^\circ\text{T}$) measures direction clockwise from North ($000^\circ\text{T}$), with East $= 090^\circ\text{T}$, South $= 180^\circ\text{T}$, and West $= 270^\circ\text{T}$. When solving navigation problems, draw a North-South-East-West compass rose at EVERY turning point or vertex. To find a back-bearing (the direction from $B$ back to $A$), add $180^\circ$ if the forward bearing is less than $180^\circ$, or subtract $180^\circ$ if the forward bearing is greater than or equal to $180^\circ$.
theory.callout_title: Read carefully: 'From' Marks the Compass Centre
theory.callout_rule: In the phrase 'the bearing of $B$ FROM $A$', the word FROM tells you where to draw the North arrow: stand at $A$, face North ($000^\circ\text{T}$), and turn clockwise until you point towards $B$.

worked_examples.title: Finding Unknown Acute Angles Using Inverse Trigonometric Functions
worked_examples.problem: Find the acute angle $\theta$ in each right-angled triangle: (a) Opposite side $O = 9\text{ cm}$ and Hypotenuse $H = 18\text{ cm}$, and (b) Adjacent side $A = 7\text{ m}$ and Opposite side $O = 7\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$.

steps.thinking: In part (a), $O$ and $H$ are given, so use $\sin\theta = \frac{O}{H}$ and apply $\sin^{-1}$.
In part (b), $O$ and $A$ are given, so use $\tan\theta = \frac{O}{A}$ and apply $\tan^{-1}$.

now_you_try.problem: A right-angled triangle has an adjacent side of $11\text{ cm}$ and an opposite side of $11\text{ cm}$. Find the acute angle $\theta$.

worked_examples.title: Cliff Lighthouse Angle of Depression Problem
worked_examples.problem: The lantern room of the Split Point Lighthouse at Aireys Inlet is $60\text{ m}$ vertically above sea level. The keeper spots a yacht at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$. Find the exact horizontal distance $d$ from the base of the cliff directly below the lighthouse to the yacht (and round to $1$ decimal place).

steps.thinking: By alternate angles between the parallel horizontal sea level and the keeper's horizontal line of sight, the angle of elevation from the yacht to the lantern room is also $30^\circ$.

now_you_try.problem: From the top of a $45\text{ m}$ observation tower, a ranger sights a campfire at a horizontal ground distance of $45\text{ m}$ from the base of the tower. What is the angle of depression from the ranger to the campfire?
now_you_try.hint: The angle of depression equals the angle of elevation $\theta$, where $\tan\theta = \frac{45}{45}$.

worked_examples.title: Navigation and True Bearings in Right-Angled Triangles
worked_examples.problem: A search-and-rescue helicopter leaves base $O$ and flies $40\text{ km}$ due North to point $A$, then turns and flies $40\sqrt{3}\text{ km}$ due East to point $B$. (a) Find the direct distance $OB$ from base $O$ to $B$. (b) Find the three-figure true bearing of $B$ from $O$, and the back-bearing of $O$ from $B$.

steps.thinking: Since North and East meet at $\angle OAB = 90^\circ$, apply Pythagoras' theorem to find $OB$.

In $\triangle OAB$, the angle $\theta = \angle AOB$ is measured clockwise from North ($OA$). Use $\tan\theta = \frac{AB}{OA}$ to find $\theta$, write it as a 3-digit bearing, and add $180^\circ$ for the back-bearing.
steps.working:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{40\sqrt{3}}{40} = \sqrt{3} \implies \theta = 60^\circ \implies \text{Bearing of } B \text{ from } O = 060^\circ\text{T}$$
$$\text{Back-bearing of } O \text{ from } B = 060^\circ + 180^\circ = 240^\circ\text{T}$$

worked_examples.final_answer: (a) $80\text{ km}$, (b) Bearing of $B$ from $O$ is $060^\circ\text{T}$; bearing of $O$ from $B$ is $240^\circ\text{T}$

now_you_try.problem: A yacht sails from port $P$ on a true bearing of $120^\circ\text{T}$ for $50\text{ km}$ to point $Q$. How far South and how far East of port $P$ is the yacht at $Q$?
now_you_try.hint: A bearing of $120^\circ\text{T}$ is $30^\circ$ South of East (or $60^\circ$ East of South).
now_you_try.working_summary: Using the $30^\circ$ angle below East: $\text{South} = 50\sin 30^\circ = 25\text{ km}$ and $\text{East} = 50\cos 30^\circ = 25\sqrt{3}\text{ km} \approx 43.30\text{ km}$.
now_you_try.answer: $25\text{ km}$ South and $25\sqrt{3}\text{ km} \approx 43.30\text{ km}$ East

common_misconceptions.title: Placing the Angle of Depression Against the Vertical Wall or Cliff
common_misconceptions.misconception: Putting the angle of depression inside the triangle between the vertical cliff face and the slanted line of sight.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Angles of elevation and depression are ALWAYS measured from the HORIZONTAL. The angle between the vertical cliff face and the line of sight is the complement $(90^\circ - \theta)$, not $\theta$.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: A shallow angle of depression like $5^\circ$ means looking almost horizontally at a very distant ship, whereas putting $5^\circ$ against the cliff places the ship almost directly underneath the cliff.

common_misconceptions.title: Measuring True Bearings from the East/West Axis Instead of North
common_misconceptions.misconception: Using an interior triangle angle measured from East or South directly as the true bearing without converting to clockwise from North ($000^\circ\text{T}$).
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: A true bearing must ALWAYS start at North ($000^\circ\text{T}$), turn clockwise, and be written with three digits. For example, $30^\circ$ South of West is $270^\circ - 30^\circ = 240^\circ\text{T}$, not $030^\circ\text{T}$.
common_misconceptions.correct_working: $$\text{South is } 180^\circ\text{T}, \text{ so } 30^\circ \text{ clockwise past South is } 180^\circ + 30^\circ = 210^\circ\text{T}.$$
common_misconceptions.counter_example: $030^\circ\text{T}$ points North-North-East, which is in the opposite hemisphere from South-South-West ($210^\circ\text{T}$).

fluency_and_understanding.question: Find the acute angle $\theta$ in a right-angled triangle if the side adjacent to $\theta$ is $12\text{ cm}$ and the hypotenuse is $24\text{ cm}$.
step_by_step_solution: Write the cosine ratio: $\cos\theta = \frac{A}{H} = \frac{12}{24} = \frac{1}{2}$.
Apply inverse cosine: $\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 60^\circ$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Find the acute angle $\theta$ in a right-angled triangle if the side opposite $\theta$ is $5\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}$ and the hypotenuse is $10\text{ cm}$.
step_by_step_solution: Write the sine ratio: $\sin\theta = \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{10} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.
Apply inverse sine: $\theta = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = 45^\circ$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Write each of the following compass directions as a three-figure true bearing: (a) $35^\circ$ East of North ($\text{N}35^\circ\text{E}$), (b) $25^\circ$ South of East, (c) $40^\circ$ West of South ($\text{S}40^\circ\text{W}$), and (d) $15^\circ$ West of North ($\text{N}15^\circ\text{W}$).
step_by_step_solution: (a) Clockwise from $000^\circ\text{T}$ gives $035^\circ\text{T}$; (b) $25^\circ$ past East ($090^\circ\text{T}$) gives $090^\circ + 25^\circ = 115^\circ\text{T}$.

(c) $40^\circ$ clockwise past South ($180^\circ\text{T}$) gives $180^\circ + 40^\circ = 220^\circ\text{T}$; (d) $15^\circ$ anticlockwise from $360^\circ\text{T}$ gives $360^\circ - 15^\circ = 345^\circ\text{T}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: The true bearing of town $B$ from town $A$ is $138^\circ\text{T}$. Find the true bearing of town $A$ from town $B$.
step_by_step_solution: Since the forward bearing $138^\circ\text{T}$ is less than $180^\circ$, add $180^\circ$ to find the opposite direction.
$\text{Back-bearing} = 138^\circ + 180^\circ = 318^\circ\text{T}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A surveyor stands $50\text{ m}$ horizontally from the base of a vertical communications tower in Canberra. Using a clinometer held at eye level $1.7\text{ m}$ above the ground, she measures the angle of elevation to the top of the tower to be $45^\circ$. Find the total height of the tower above the ground.
step_by_step_solution: Find the vertical rise $h$ above eye level: $h = 50 \tan 45^\circ = 50 \times 1 = 50\text{ m}$.
Add the surveyor's eye height of $1.7\text{ m}$: $\text{Total height} = 50 + 1.7 = 51.7\text{ m}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: An bushfire spotter plane is flying at a constant altitude of $600\text{ m}$ above flat ground in Gippsland. The pilot spots a plume of smoke at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$. What is the direct line-of-sight distance from the plane to the base of the smoke plume?
step_by_step_solution: The vertical altitude $O = 600\text{ m}$ is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle of elevation/depression, and the direct line-of-sight distance is the hypotenuse $H$.
Solve $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{600}{H} \implies H = \frac{600}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{600}{0.5} = 1200\text{ m}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A bushwalker hikes $18\text{ km}$ on a true bearing of $210^\circ\text{T}$ from campsite $C$ to lookout $L$. How far South and how far West of campsite $C$ is lookout $L$?
problem_solving_and_modelling.final_answer: $9\sqrt{3}\text{ km} \approx 15.59\text{ km}$ South and $9\text{ km}$ West
step_by_step_solution: A bearing of $210^\circ\text{T}$ makes an angle of $210^\circ - 180^\circ = 30^\circ$ West of South.
In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $18\text{ km}$, $\text{South} = 18\cos 30^\circ = 9\sqrt{3}\text{ km} \approx 15.59\text{ km}$ and $\text{West} = 18\sin 30^\circ = 9\text{ km}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: Two ships leave Fremantle harbour at the same time. Ship $A$ sails on a bearing of $040^\circ\text{T}$ for $15\text{ km}$, while Ship $B$ sails on a bearing of $130^\circ\text{T}$ for $20\text{ km}$. Show that their paths are perpendicular ($90^\circ$) and find the direct distance between the two ships.
step_by_step_solution: The angle between bearings $040^\circ\text{T}$ and $130^\circ\text{T}$ is $130^\circ - 40^\circ = 90^\circ$, forming a right-angled triangle.
By Pythagoras' theorem, $d = \sqrt{15^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{225 + 400} = \sqrt{625} = 25\text{ km}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: A student enters $\sin^{-1}(1.4)$ into her calculator and receives a 'MATH ERROR'. Explain geometrically why $\sin^{-1}(x)$ and $\cos^{-1}(x)$ are undefined whenever $|x| > 1$, whereas $\tan^{-1}(x)$ is defined for all real numbers $x$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: In a right-angled triangle, $O < H$ and $A < H$, so $\sin\theta = \frac{O}{H}$ and $\cos\theta = \frac{A}{H}$ can never exceed $1$; however, $\frac{O}{A}$ can take any positive value
step_by_step_solution: Because the hypotenuse $H$ is strictly the longest side of any right-angled triangle, neither $\frac{O}{H}$ nor $\frac{A}{H}$ can ever be $1.4 > 1$.
By contrast, the ratio of the two legs $\tan\theta = \frac{O}{A}$ can be arbitrarily large as $\theta$ approaches $90^\circ$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: From a boat at point $A$, the angle of elevation to the top of a vertical $60\text{ m}$ coastal cliff is $30^\circ$. The boat then sails directly towards the cliff to point $B$, where the angle of elevation to the top of the cliff is now $60^\circ$. Find the exact distance $AB$ that the boat sailed.
step_by_step_solution: At point $A$, horizontal distance from the cliff base is $d_A = \frac{60}{\tan 30^\circ} = 60\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$. At point $B$, horizontal distance is $d_B = \frac{60}{\tan 60^\circ} = \frac{60}{\sqrt{3}} = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$.
Subtracting gives the distance sailed: $AB = d_A - d_B = 60\sqrt{3} - 20\sqrt{3} = 40\sqrt{3}\text{ m} \approx 69.28\text{ m}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: A rectangular prism has base dimensions $4\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm}$ and vertical height $5\text{ cm}$. Find the angle of elevation $\theta$ that the internal 3D space diagonal makes with the horizontal $4\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm}$ base floor.
step_by_step_solution: First find the horizontal base diagonal using Pythagoras' theorem: $d_{\text{floor}} = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\text{ cm}$.
In the vertical right-angled triangle formed by $d_{\text{floor}} = 5\text{ cm}$ and vertical height $h = 5\text{ cm}$, $\tan\theta = \frac{5}{5} = 1 \implies \theta = 45^\circ$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Two observation towers $A$ and $B$ of heights $20\text{ m}$ and $50\text{ m}$ stand on flat ground $30\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$ apart. Find (a) the angle of elevation from the top of tower $A$ to the top of tower $B$, and (b) the direct distance between their tops.
step_by_step_solution: The vertical height difference between the tops is $\Delta h = 50 - 20 = 30\text{ m}$, and the horizontal separation is $30\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$.
Thus $\tan\theta = \frac{30}{30\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \implies \theta = 30^\circ$, and the direct distance is $d = \frac{30}{\sin 30^\circ} = 60\text{ m}$.
